# Locating and Diagnosing the Engine Temperature Sensor on a Mazda 323

On a 2003 Mazda 323 Astina equipped with the 1.8L engine, the primary coolant temperature sensor is typically mounted directly onto the cylinder head near the thermostat housing. This placement is intentional; by sitting in the hottest part of the cooling loop, it provides the Engine Control Unit (ECU) with real-time data necessary for fuel mixture adjustments and ignition timing. In many Mazda models of this era, there are actually two sensors: one for the ECU to manage engine performance, and a second dedicated sensor that feeds directly into the dashboard gauge cluster. If your goal is to fix the overheating or fan logic issues you described, verifying the location of the correct sensor is the first logical step.

The symptoms you listedâcoolant boiling under load and the radiator fan failing to engage while the A/C compressor continues to runâpoint strongly toward a failure in the ECU-side temperature circuit rather than a mechanical blockage. The fact that the A/C fan works confirms that the electrical system has power and the fan motor itself is functional; the issue lies in the control logic. The ECU uses the voltage signal from the coolant sensor to determine when to activate the electric radiator fan. When the sensor reads a temperature higher than the threshold (usually around 90Â°C to 100Â°C), it should command the relay to close the circuit to the fan. If the sensor is faulty, stuck in an "open" state, or has high resistance, the ECU may interpret this as cold coolant and never trigger the fan.

To diagnose the fault without replacing parts immediately, you need to understand how these sensors report data. Most automotive coolant temperature sensors use a Negative Temperature Coefficient (NTC) thermistor. As the engine heats up, the resistance of the thermistor drops. Conversely, when the engine is cold, the resistance is very high. A multimeter can help verify this behavior. With the ignition on but the engine off, you can probe the sensor connector at the cylinder head. You should see a relatively high resistance reading (often between 2kÎ© and 5kÎ© depending on the specific model year). As you gently warm the sensor with your hands or a heat gun, the resistance should drop smoothly. If the reading is infinite (open circuit) or stuck at zero, the sensor has failed internally.

Another critical pitfall is confusing the ECU sensor with the gauge cluster sensor. They are often identical parts, but they serve different control functions. Swapping a working gauge sensor into the ECU port might not resolve the fan issue if the ECU expects a specific resistance curve that only the original part provides. Furthermore, corrosion at the connector pins is a common cause of erratic readings. Inspect the wiring harness near the thermostat housing for signs of chafing or melted insulation, which can happen due to the heat cycle of the engine bay.

If you decide to replace the sensor, ensure you use the correct part number specified for the 1.8L Astina chassis code. A poor ground connection at the sensor plug can also mimic a failed sensor, so check the integrity of the ground strap before condemning the thermistor itself. Addressing this electrical fault is often more cost-effective than replacing the water pump or radiator if those components are still in good mechanical condition.
